label: Sleep duration
why_in_space: Astronaut studies from Shuttle and Mir missions report shorter sleep in flight. Short sleep goes together with fatigue and slower performance, so your own trend matters more than one night.
how_to_measure: Log the hours you slept each morning, or import them from a wrist device if the crew has one.

yellow: Protect a fixed sleep window tonight.
Note it and check again tomorrow.
red: Keep your sleep window fixed and quiet.
Tell the crew medical officer today.
Ask the flight surgeon for guidance.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.
notes: The 2009 evidence is small-sample and historical. Thresholds must come from a cited source or stay as deviation from personal baseline.

label: Sleep quality
why_in_space: Small astronaut studies report changes in sleep quality and continuity in flight, but not in the same direction for every measure or mission.
how_to_measure: Rate how rested you feel each morning on a 1-5 scale (app-defined scale).

yellow: Note light, noise and temperature in your sleep area.
red: Tell the crew medical officer today.
Ask the flight surgeon for guidance.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.

label: Sleep timing
why_in_space: Circadian timing and lighting are linked to sleep and alertness in flight studies. Keeping timing steady helps read your sleep data correctly.
how_to_measure: Log the time you went to sleep and woke up.

yellow: Keep sleep and wake times as steady as the schedule allows.
red: Tell the crew medical officer today.
Ask the flight surgeon for guidance.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.

label: Crew cohesion and mood
why_in_space: Isolation and confinement can affect how crew members get along. Direct astronaut evidence is limited, so the app follows each person's own trend instead of assuming a dip at a fixed date.
how_to_measure: Answer a short daily check-in about mood, team relations and support (app-defined scale).

yellow: Talk with a crew member you trust.
Note what changed in the schedule or workload.
red: Tell the crew medical officer today.
Ask the flight surgeon for guidance.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.

label: Reaction time
why_in_space: Short repeated reaction tests compared with your own baseline are how NASA tracks alertness and performance. Slower reactions can show up before you feel tired.
how_to_measure: Do the 1-3 minute reaction self-test at the same time of day.

yellow: Check your sleep trend: the two often move together.
red: Avoid safety-critical tasks alone.
Tell the crew medical officer today.
Ask the flight surgeon for guidance.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.
notes: No evidence card yet in hazards.json. Add one from Roma 2018 / Nasrini 2020 once opened.

label: Exercise time
why_in_space: Exercise is the countermeasure used consistently against muscle atrophy and strength loss in microgravity. The 2009 report describes about 2.5 hours per day on six days a week on the ISS (setup and hygiene included).
how_to_measure: Log minutes of resistance and aerobic exercise each day.

yellow: Protect your exercise slot in the day plan.
red: Tell the crew medical officer about missed sessions.
Ask the flight surgeon for guidance.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.

label: Muscle strength
why_in_space: Microgravity is associated with muscle atrophy and lower strength and endurance. The chapter gives no quantitative muscle-loss estimate, so only the change from your own baseline is meaningful.
how_to_measure: Protocol to be defined by the team: repeat the same simple strength check on a fixed schedule.

yellow: Note it and check again tomorrow.
Compare with your own baseline in the trend chart.
red: Tell the crew medical officer today.
Ask the flight surgeon for guidance.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.
notes: Needs a defined, safe measurement protocol before it can be a real input.

label: Calcium (blood)

thresholds.range_note: Most frequent lab range per sex in LSDS-8 (C003 pre-flight rows excluded). A lab range is not a diagnosis.

why_in_space: Calcium is part of the metabolic panel NASA measured in crew before and after flight (LSDS-8).
how_to_measure: Lab value from a blood panel; not measurable by the crew member alone.

yellow: Note the value and the date.
red: Tell the crew medical officer today.
Ask the flight surgeon for guidance.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.

label: Resting heart rate
why_in_space: Pulse is a quick whole-body signal. A resting rate that moves away from your own baseline, especially together with fever, deserves attention.
how_to_measure: Camera pulse (rPPG) or manual count while resting. Compare with a pulse oximeter or a manual count before trusting the camera.

yellow: Rest 5 minutes and measure again.
red: Tell the crew medical officer today.
Ask the flight surgeon for guidance.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.
notes: No source yet for a threshold. Camera accuracy still to be tested with a real person.

label: Blood pressure (systolic)
why_in_space: Hypertension is listed among possible late cardiovascular concerns of space radiation, but the 2009 evidence comes from non-astronaut populations. Treat this as a research gap, not a proven in-flight effect.
how_to_measure: Cuff measurement, seated and rested, at the same time of day.

yellow: Rest and measure again.
red: Tell the crew medical officer today.
Ask the flight surgeon for guidance.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.
notes: Evidence gap card: do not present as a demonstrated astronaut outcome.

label: Body temperature
why_in_space: Fever is a simple sign of infection or inflammation. Medical help is far away, so a fever is worth reporting early.
how_to_measure: Oral or forehead thermometer at the same time of day.

yellow: Measure again in an hour.
Drink fluids and rest.
red: Tell the crew medical officer today.
Ask the flight surgeon for guidance.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.
notes: No source yet for a threshold.

label: Blood glucose

thresholds.range_note: Most frequent lab range per sex in LSDS-8 (C003 pre-flight rows excluded). A lab range is not a diagnosis.

why_in_space: Glucose regulation is part of the metabolic picture, but the 2009 chapter gives no astronaut glucose result. In LSDS-8, the very low values at R+45 are probably sample artifacts (late processing), not a finding.
how_to_measure: Lab value from a blood panel; not measurable by the crew member alone.

yellow: Note the value and the date.
red: Tell the crew medical officer today.
Ask the flight surgeon for guidance.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.
notes: Four QC-flagged points in the NASA data (3 glucose, 1 potassium) are excluded from baselines.

label: Creatinine (blood)

thresholds.range_note: Most frequent lab range per sex in LSDS-8 (C003 pre-flight rows excluded). A lab range is not a diagnosis.

why_in_space: Creatinine is a kidney-related marker in the metabolic panel NASA measured before and after flight (LSDS-8).
how_to_measure: Lab value from a blood panel; not measurable by the crew member alone.

yellow: Note the value and the date.
red: Tell the crew medical officer today.
Ask the flight surgeon for guidance.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.
notes: No kidney system in the 6 categories of hazards.json; kept under immune_metabolic.

label: Light flashes
why_in_space: Astronauts have reported brief light flashes (phosphenes) since Apollo, and they were studied on Skylab, Mir and the ISS. They are subjective and do not by themselves show brain injury.
how_to_measure: Count how many flashes you noticed today and note the context.

yellow: Log the time and where you were.
red: Tell the crew medical officer today.
Ask the flight surgeon for guidance.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.
notes: Not a diagnostic marker of CNS injury.

label: Radiation dose (modeled)
why_in_space: Solar particle events are a potential acute radiation hazard for crews. The 2009 assessment is model-based: it does not report confirmed acute radiation syndrome in astronauts.
how_to_measure: From the environment feed or the simulation; not measured by the crew member.

yellow: Follow the radiation shelter plan for the habitat.
red: Go to the shelter area per mission procedure.
Tell the crew medical officer today.
Ask the flight surgeon for guidance.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.
notes: Unit and source of the app's dose still to confirm with the simulation. Replace simulated dose with real data when possible.

label: Chromosome exchanges
why_in_space: In 24 astronauts, blood samples taken before and after flight showed more chromosome exchanges. This is a biological marker, not a cancer diagnosis.
how_to_measure: Not measured by the app. Laboratory analysis of blood samples.
escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.

label: Brain function (radiation risk)
why_in_space: The 2009 chapter found no identified radiation-related brain effects in astronauts, and said reliable risk projections were not possible. Absence of evidence is not proof of no risk.
how_to_measure: Not measured directly. Reaction time and sleep are the practical daily signals.
escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.

label: Lunar dust symptoms
why_in_space: Apollo crews described lunar dust irritating the eyes, throat and nose. Effects of long exposure are uncertain.
how_to_measure: Rate eye, throat and nose irritation after EVA (app-defined scale).

yellow: Clean suit and boots before entering the habitat.
red: Tell the crew medical officer today.
Ask the flight surgeon for guidance.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.
notes: Historical observations, not a controlled study.

label: Dust contact events
why_in_space: Dust can enter the habitat on suits and boots after EVA, during suit cleaning and when filters are changed. These are exposure pathways, not measured doses.
how_to_measure: Log EVAs, suit-cleaning and filter-change tasks.

yellow: Follow the suit-cleaning and ingress procedure.
red: Tell the crew medical officer today.
Ask the flight surgeon for guidance.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.

label: Workspace accessibility
why_in_space: Accumulated stowage can block translation paths, panels and equipment, which matters for efficiency and emergency access.
how_to_measure: Rate access to routes and equipment in your module.

yellow: Clear the blocked route or report it.
red: Report a blocked emergency route immediately.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.

label: Suit discomfort
why_in_space: In ground tests, participants reported suit discomfort that increased when pressurized. This is indirect evidence: participants were not confirmed as flight astronauts.
how_to_measure: Rate discomfort by body region after suit use.

yellow: Report the area and the activity.
red: Tell the crew medical officer today.
Ask the flight surgeon for guidance.

escalate_when: Any red result, or any yellow that keeps getting worse for several days.
notes: Indirect human testing: keep out of the astronaut-only core evidence.
